title: India's $18 Billion Semiconductor Bet Takes Shape as China Rewrites the Chips Playbook
excerpt: With Micron operational, Tata's fab targeting late 2026, and ISM 2.0 expanding scope, India is racing to build chip sovereignty — but the gap with global leaders remains vast.
body:
• India has committed roughly $18 billion across 10 semiconductor projects in six states, anchored by the India Semiconductor Mission's ₹76,000 crore outlay offering up to 50% fiscal support.
  • Micron's $2.75 billion assembly and test facility in Sanand, Gujarat was inaugurated in February 2026. Tata's $11 billion fabrication plant in Dholera with Taiwan's PSMC targets late 2026.
  • ISM 2.0, announced in the 2026–27 budget, expands focus to semiconductor equipment, materials, IP development, and supply chain resilience.
  • India imports 85% of its semiconductors and has no domestic EDA tools, with demand projected to hit $100 billion by 2030.

From Announcements to Construction

India's semiconductor push is moving from PowerPoint to concrete. Micron's $2.75 billion assembly, test, marking, and packaging facility in Sanand, Gujarat became operational in February 2026, according to industry reports. Tata's $11 billion fabrication plant in Dholera, built in partnership with Taiwan's Powerchip Semiconductor Manufacturing Corporation, is targeting a late 2026 launch. AMD has established its largest global design centre in Bengaluru, and Lam Research has committed $1 billion in Karnataka.

Across six states, ten projects are in various stages of construction or pilot production, per the Economic Times. The India Semiconductor Mission, with an outlay of ₹76,000 crore, offers up to 50% fiscal support for approved fabrication projects — among the most generous incentive structures globally, according to Livemint.

ISM 2.0 Broadens the Scope

The 2026–27 Union Budget introduced ISM 2.0, expanding the mission beyond manufacturing to encompass semiconductor equipment, materials, intellectual property development, and supply chain resilience. The shift recognises that building isolated fabrication units is insufficient — India needs an integrated ecosystem spanning design, manufacturing, and packaging, per Livemint.

India already contributes significantly to one link in the chain: approximately 20% of the world's chip design talent works in India, mostly for multinationals like Qualcomm, Intel, and AMD. What the country has lacked is the factory, the equipment, and the materials to complete the circuit.

The China Factor

India's semiconductor urgency is partly driven by China's aggressive moves in the same space. Despite US export controls restricting access to advanced chipmaking equipment and processors, China has continued to invest heavily in mature-node chip production and is exploring workarounds for advanced AI chips, according to Outlook Business.

The global semiconductor supply chain remains dangerously concentrated. Taiwan alone accounts for roughly 90% of advanced chip production. The COVID-era chip shortage demonstrated the cascading economic damage when supply is disrupted, affecting 169 industries across the global economy.

"India imports 85% of its semiconductors, making it vulnerable to global disruptions. With demand projected to reach $100 billion by 2030, building a local chip ecosystem is vital for national security, economic resilience, and digital autonomy."

— Outlook Business

What's Missing

For all the momentum, the gaps remain significant. India has no domestic electronic design automation tools — the software that underpins chip architecture. There is no real ecosystem for chip intellectual property. The country's first indigenously fabricated chip, expected in mid-2025, uses older technology compared to today's most advanced nodes, Outlook Business reported.

The supply chain India needs — specialty chemicals, ultra-pure gases, photomasks, advanced packaging substrates — largely does not exist domestically. Building it will take years, substantial capital, and technical partnerships that extend beyond the headline investments.

Diaspora and Talent Pipeline

Indian semiconductor professionals working at TSMC, Intel, Samsung, and other global firms represent a critical talent bridge. Several senior executives in India's new fab projects are returned diaspora engineers. For NRI professionals in the chip industry, the build-out creates career pathways that did not exist five years ago — from process engineering in Dholera to design verification in Bengaluru.

What to Watch

Execution is everything. Taiwan built its semiconductor industry over 30 years. India is attempting a compressed timeline with government subsidies substituting for decades of organic ecosystem development. The Tata-PSMC fab in Dholera is the bellwether — if it delivers on time and at scale, it validates India's approach. If it delays, the credibility gap widens.
